01
01 · The Question

Since childhood, I've been fascinated by machines, not just how they move, but how they sense, decide, and adapt.

That curiosity has shaped a research path spanning control theory, mechanics, dynamics, and robotic actuation, all converging on one question.

How do we design systems that perceive uncertainty and respond intelligently, especially when they interact directly with people?

As heavy machinery. As rig control systems. As soft robotic actuators. As prosthetic hands.

02

03
03 · The Detour

Then I took on a different kind of problem.

As a Graduate Research Assistant with Dr. Eric van Oort and Dr. Dongmei Chen at UT Austin, I'm designing a real-time control system for a fluid-handling platform where the working fluid's rheology shifts unpredictably over time: the drill mud mixing process in oil & gas well drilling.

I treated it as a general real-time nonlinear control and state-estimation problem: implementing MPC, LQR, and Kalman filtering on embedded hardware to stabilize a system with highly uncertain, time-varying dynamics.

It reinforced that the tools I care about most (real-time estimation, optimization-based control, hardware integration) transfer across applications. View the project →

Automated Drill Mud Mixing System

The University of Texas at Austin, MINIMAX Lab, with Dr. Eric van Oort & Dr. Dongmei Chen · Jan 2026 – Present
Overview

Drilling mud, the fluid circulated through a well during drilling, has to be mixed to precise density, viscosity, and chemical specifications in real time. Getting it wrong can mean anything from inefficient drilling to a serious well-control incident. This project is building a Level-4 automated control system for the mud mixing process, moving it from manual, operator-supervised batching toward closed-loop automated control.

Details

My work spans process modeling, control system design, and safety-focused automation logic, with an emphasis on reliability under the kind of variable, imperfectly known conditions that show up on an actual rig rather than a clean simulation. It's a deliberate departure from my soft-materials work in scale and domain, but the underlying problem, controlling a system that doesn't behave linearly or predictably, is the same one I keep coming back to.

Soft GI-Tract Phantom Using Dielectric Elastomers

The University of Texas at Austin, MINIMAX Lab, with Dr. Fangzhou Xia · Mar 2025 – Present
Overview

The gastrointestinal tract moves in ways that are difficult to replicate with rigid or purely passive materials: localized wall contraction, distension, and peristaltic waves driven by internal pressure. This project develops a hemispherical balloon dielectric elastomer actuator designed to reproduce that motion for capsule-endoscopy phantom research: physical stand-ins for GI anatomy used to test ingestible devices without involving live subjects.

Details

The actuator is a 1 mm 3M VHB 4910 membrane clamped over a 55 mm bore, modeled with a Mooney–Rivlin hyperelastic formulation (C10 = 15 kPa, C01 = 5 kPa) and driven by combined pneumatic pressure (1–5 kPa) and Maxwell stress. Visible actuation begins around 7–8 kV: at low pressure the response stays radial, with curvature changing near 9.6 kV; at higher pressure it shifts to a localized, apex-dominated bulge near 10.2 kV. This work was presented at the 2026 IEEE/ASME International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics (AIM) in Genova, Italy.

Dielectric Elastomer Bending Actuators for Finger-like Gripping

Indian Institute of Technology, Jodhpur, with Dr. Atul Kumar Sharma · 2024 – 2025
Overview

This project grew out of a simple question: given a huge space of possible actuator geometries, prestretch ratios, and electrode layouts, which designs actually bend reliably, and which fail? Over more than forty fabricated dielectric elastomer bending actuators, I varied dielectric film thickness, prestretch ratio, electrode segmentation, and actuator dimensions, then tested each one under high-voltage excitation to identify which combinations produced stable, repeatable bending versus dielectric breakdown, electrode shorting, or no response at all.

Details

Only 4 of 25 fully characterized designs held up (an ~18% success rate), but the best performer bent past 60° at roughly 8.66 kV, and catastrophic breakdown (visible sparking, occasionally ignition) was the most common failure mode at reduced edge spacing. That motivated the second half of the project: training a linear SVM classifier on nine geometric features (film thickness, prestretch ratios, electrode layout, actuator dimensions, edge spacing) to screen candidate designs before fabrication, reaching ~83% classification accuracy. This manuscript was accepted for publication in physica status solidi (a) and was presented at the RAMAN 2026 conference in Ahmedabad.

Circular DEA: Nonlinear Deformation Based on Gent's Elasticity Theory

Indian Institute of Technology, Jodhpur, with Dr. Atul Kumar Sharma · 2025
Overview

This study examined how well a Gent hyperelastic model (built to capture the strain-stiffening that comes from finite polymer chain extensibility) predicts the actual voltage-stretch behavior of circular dielectric elastomer actuators across different pre-stretch ratios. Four planar circular DEA specimens (3M VHB 4905, shear modulus 24.5 kPa) were fabricated at radial pre-stretch ratios from 2.5 to 3.7, mounted on rigid frames, and driven by a Trek high-voltage amplifier ramping a triangular waveform up to 10 kV while a Laser Doppler Vibrometer logged roughly 200,000 displacement points per cycle.

Details

The analytical model matched the experimental data most closely at a pre-stretch ratio of 3.0 (a predicted peak displacement of 2.7 mm against a measured 2.6 mm), but diverged more noticeably at higher pre-stretch and voltage levels, pointing to dielectric saturation and viscoelastic effects the current model doesn't capture. That gap is where this line of work is headed next. This manuscript is currently submitted for publication.

Upper-Limb Prosthesis & Assistive Devices

Institute of Technology, Nirma University, with Dr. Reena Trivedi · 2022 – 2024
Overview

This was my introduction to soft robotics as an undergraduate, and it stayed a throughline for the research I've done since. The first phase built SMA and pneumatic finger-like actuators for upper-limb prosthetics, driven by electromyography (EMG) signals from the user's residual muscles. Cylindrical-trained SMA wire reached bending angles of 64°±5% (PIP) and 68°±5% (DIP), with real-time EMG control averaging a 0.9s response (about 0.075s of electronic delay plus 0.35s of SMA heating) and under 5% deviation across repeated trials. That work led to two peer-reviewed publications, linked ahead.

Details

A related project extended the same EMG-driven approach into a soft, fiber-reinforced pneumatic finger actuator (3D-printed and silicone-molded) controlled by a custom PID loop that held it within about 0.5° of a 32.6° target at 14.4 kPa, tested across four individuals over repeated grip cycles. Both threads fed into a soft robotic assistive glove for stroke and motor-neuron-disease patients, built for ROBOFEST 3.0, a national robotics competition hosted by GujCOST.

Two-Wheeled Self-Balancing Robot

Institute of Technology, Nirma University · Apr – May 2023
Overview

A classic control problem, built from scratch: a two-wheeled robot in an inverted-pendulum configuration that has to actively balance itself rather than relying on a wide wheelbase. I used an Arduino Uno paired with an MPU6050 inertial measurement unit (accelerometer + gyroscope) to estimate tilt angle in real time, and a closed-loop control routine to drive the two motors and continuously counteract that tilt.

Details

Beyond basic balance, the robot was tested through a full 360° rotation to confirm the controller stayed stable through sustained turning, not just quiet standing balance. It's a small project, but it's where I first got hands-on with the sensor fusion and feedback-control ideas that show up in a lot of my later work.
